programme: BMAL1 (core circadian clock transcription factor, paired with CLOCK) and SIRT1 (its NAD+-dependent deacetylase partner) form a circadian-redox/DNA-damage axis: BMAL1/CLOCK drive rhythmic transcription and directly support double-strand-break repair, while SIRT1 senses metabolic/oxidative state and feeds back onto the same clock output to control cell survival under genotoxic or hypoxic stress.
role_in_a: In osteosarcoma, BMAL1 (with CLOCK) directly promotes DNA double-strand-break repair and drives chemoresistance, and the core clock supports cancer stem cell survival and EMT-like behavior; SIRT1 is independently implicated in oncogenic network/metabolic rewiring in sarcoma.
role_in_b: In stroke, BMAL1 protects neural tissue against transient focal cerebral ischemia, and SIRT1 acts through the SIRT1/AMPK/PGC1α axis to support mitochondrial and neuroprotective signaling in ischemic injury and against intracranial aneurysm rupture.
shared_axis: Both an ischemic brain and a genotoxically-stressed tumor depend on a stress-adaptive circadian-redox circuit to decide whether cells repair and survive or die; sarcoma appears to co-opt the same BMAL1-SIRT1 circuit that the ischemic brain uses for protection, repurposing a damage-response programme for chemoresistance instead of neuroprotection.
reasoning: No retrieved paper studies sarcoma and stroke together, so this is not an established shared axis, but the record independently and specifically places both BMAL1 and SIRT1 in disease-relevant processes in sarcoma (DNA repair, stemness) and in stroke (ischemic neuroprotection), and the BMAL1-SIRT1 partnership is a recognized circadian-metabolic module, not an arbitrary pairing. That both carrying factors are placed on both sides of the pair, with reasonably high recurrence (17/30 each), pushes this past moderate.
support: 40214471 (BMAL1/CLOCK regulate osteosarcoma stem cell survival via CSC/EMT pathways); 36725890 (BMAL1 collaborates with CLOCK to promote DNA double-strand-break repair and chemoresistance in tumor cells); 41005429 (Bmal1 protects against transient focal cerebral ischemia in mice); 42032714 (bioinformatics/network toxicology implicating SIRT1 mechanisms in sarcoma); 42544484 (Sirtuin-1 prevents intracranial aneurysm rupture in mice); 42246162 (SIRT1/AMPK/PGC1α pathway reviewed as neuroprotective in ischemic stroke)
how_to_falsify: In an osteosarcoma cell line with documented BMAL1-driven chemoresistance, pharmacologically inhibit SIRT1 (e.g. EX-527) or knock it down and test whether BMAL1-mediated double-strand-break repair and chemoresistance are unaffected; in parallel, in a mouse cerebral ischemia-reperfusion model, knock out BMAL1 and ask whether SIRT1/AMPK/PGC1α-mediated neuroprotection still occurs unchanged. If the two factors act independently in either tissue rather than through a coupled clock-deacetylase circuit, the shared-axis account is wrong.
caveats: The network was built on blood expression for stroke and soft-tissue expression for sarcoma, not brain tissue directly, so ischemic neuroprotection is inferred through peripheral/blood-proxy signal rather than neuronal data. Only 6 independent cohort pairs underlie the 30 patient-group comparisons, and BMAL1/SIRT1 each recur in only 17/30 (roughly half), which is respectable but not near-universal. The tissue-generic exclusion list is dominated by immune transcription factors (STAT1, SPI1, IRF1, IRF8, IKZF1, CIITA, NFATC1), consistent with blood being an immune-heavy tissue and suggesting the surviving BMAL1/SIRT1 signal is not just an immune-composition artifact. KDM2B and PITX1 also have real independent evidence in both diseases (sarcoma gene fusions/tumor suppression; stroke via ferroptosis-linked SLC7A11 regulation and HIF-1α hypoxia response respectively) but were left out of the carrying set because no documented mechanistic link ties them to the BMAL1-SIRT1 circuit specifically — naming them as part of the same programme would overreach.
